new_statements.translation: 2.1.5. Prosody. Damana is an accentual (stress) language. The nucleus of the word is the syllable that receives the greatest sonorous energy. Stress in Damana has no distinctive function. The stress zone of the word is the penultimate syllable; however, stress can move according to the following rules: – When a word has a devoiced vowel as the syllabic nucleus of its penultimate syllable, stress shifts to the final syllable: /kəˈsa/ 'foot', /kuiˈka/ 'nit'. – When a word takes a functional (case) suffix, stress moves in search of its zone [i.e. stays penultimate]: /ˈmama/ 'grandfather' : /maˈmamba/ 'for grandfather'; /uˈraga/ 'house' : /uraˈgamba/ 'in the house'; /ˈade/ 'father' : /aˈdenʒe/ 'of father'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and falls on the penultimate syllable of the word including functional suffixes (stress re-positions itself to the new penult under suffixation); if the penultimate vowel is devoiced (high/central vowels between voiceless obstruents), stress falls on the final syllable instead.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Same section: 'Es frecuente que en los polisílabos se ubiquen dos acentos: uno primario y otro secundario, sobre todo en palabras compuestas: /ˌdunˈzisi/ 'paloma', /ʃiˌmənˈkəla/ 'cabuya'' -- polysyllables, especially compounds, often have a secondary stress before the primary (position not further specified).
new_statements.exceptions: Final stress when the penult nucleus is a devoiced vowel (kəˈsa 'pie', kuiˈka 'liendre'). Williams 1993:5 fn.2 separately notes ergative -ga and compound boundaries as exceptions to a prenasalization rule, not to stress; Williams 1993:80 uses penultimate stress on mesá-ka as evidence that -ka is inside the stress domain.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the word including case/functional suffixes and clitic postpositions (Trillos: maˈmamba, uraˈgamba; Williams 1993:80 mesáka). Statements are based on citation forms; Williams adds that question intonation high pitch starts at the stressed syllable of the focused word (p. 127).
new_statements.identity_note: Both opened sources describe Damana as spoken by the Wiwa (also called Arsario, Malayo, Sanká, Guamaca, Marocasero); Glottolog mala1522 is a single language-level languoid with no listed dialects. Trillos Amaya's data come from communities around Avingüe (Cesar); Williams' from Avingüí and Santa Marta. Same variety; no dialect split reported.

new_statements.relation_note: Consistent with the existing statement (Trillos Amaya 2000 sec. 2.1.5: penultimate, non-distinctive, shifts with devoiced penult, re-placed by suffixes). Williams's incidental 'penultimate stress on mesaka' presupposes penultimate word stress and that a cliticized postposition is inside the stress domain, which matches Trillos Amaya's remark that suffixes re-place the accent. It adds nothing on secondary stress or non-contrastiveness. Confidence is low because the statement is an aside in a syntax argument, not a description of the stress system.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No explicit stress rule is given anywhere in the thesis; phonology is deferred to a separate work (C. Williams, 'A phonology of Damana', in preparation). The only word-stress evidence is incidental: the author argues that -ka 'in/on' is a clitic because the word mesa-ka bears penultimate stress (i.e. on -sa-), which presupposes that Damana word stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word including clitics. Sec. 10.1.4 adds that question intonation is a high pitch starting on the stressed syllable of the focused word, and declaratives end in a pitch fall.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the mesaka remark implies that enclitics (-ka locative) count toward the stress domain. Note p. 4 that high vowels devoice between voiceless obstruents, which is the environment Trillos Amaya 2000 gives for stress shifting to the final syllable, but Williams does not connect it to stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Williams 1993 calls the language Dəməna/Damana, 'the language of the Uiua people' of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta (p. 1), with outsider names Uiua, Arsario, Malayo, Sanha, Sanka; data gathered 1986-88 in Avingue and Santa Marta (p. 4). Same language as Trillos Amaya's damana (lengua de los wiwas, a.k.a. arsarios/malayos) = Glottolog mala1522; no dialect is singled out.

sources.note: Sec. 2.1.5 Prosodia (p. 752): Damana is an accentual language; stress is not distinctive; the stress zone is the penultimate syllable; stress moves to the final syllable when the penult has a devoiced vowel; under suffixation of a functional marker stress shifts to stay penultimate (ˈmama > maˈmamba, uˈraga > uraˈgamba); polysyllables, especially compounds, often carry a primary plus a secondary stress (ˌdunˈzisi, ʃiˌmənˈkəla). Sec. 2.1.1 also says the syllable is the stress-bearing unit and consonants never bear stress.
